tagline: Paul's shortest letter: a personal appeal to a Christian slave owner to receive his returning slave, Onesimus, as a beloved brother.
overview:
Philemon is a single page of papyrus, the shortest of Paul's surviving letters and the most personal. Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a believer who hosts a church in his house, about Onesimus, a slave who belonged to Philemon and who has come to faith through Paul while Paul was in chains. Paul is sending Onesimus back. The whole letter is an appeal for how Philemon should receive him: not merely as returning property, but "as a beloved brother" (verse 16), and even as he would receive Paul himself.

The letter is short, but it is carefully argued. Paul could command, and says so, but chooses to appeal. He offers to pay any debt Onesimus owes, reminds Philemon of his own debt to Paul, writes in front of the whole house church, and ends by asking for a guest room, since he hopes to visit. Every move puts gentle and public pressure on Philemon to act out of love rather than compulsion.

The letter matters for two reasons. It shows the gospel reaching into the most ordinary and most unequal relationship in the Roman household, the bond between master and slave, and refusing to leave it unchanged. And it has a long and painful history of use: it was cited in the nineteenth century both to defend the return of fugitive slaves and to argue that the gospel undermines slavery itself. Reading it honestly means facing both what Paul said and what he did not say.
author: The letter names Paul as its author, with Timothy joining in the greeting, and Paul signs part of it with his own hand (verse 19). Its authenticity is about as secure as anything in the study of the New Testament. Even scholars who doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, Ephesians, or the Pastoral Letters count Philemon among the seven undisputed letters. It was included in Marcion's list of Paul's letters in the second century and in the Muratorian list of accepted writings, usually dated to the late second century. Its brevity and personal subject led a few in the fourth century to question whether it belonged in Scripture at all, and writers such as Jerome and John Chrysostom defended its place, arguing that small letters can carry large truths.
date: Paul writes as a prisoner (verses 1, 9, 10, 13), but the letter does not say where. The traditional view places it during his house arrest in Rome, around AD 60 to 62, which would make it contemporary with Colossians and perhaps Ephesians and Philippians. Many scholars prefer an imprisonment in Ephesus in the mid-50s, pointing out that Ephesus is only about 120 miles (190 km) from Colossae, which makes Onesimus's arrival there and Paul's hope of a quick visit (verse 22) easier to picture. Acts does not record an Ephesian imprisonment, but Paul speaks of many imprisonments (2 Corinthians 11:23). A smaller group suggests Caesarea, around AD 57 to 59. The meaning of the letter does not depend on settling the question.
setting:
Philemon lived in or near Colossae, a town in the Lycus valley of the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey today), near Laodicea and Hierapolis. The link comes from Colossians, which names Onesimus as "one of you" and sends a charge to Archippus, both people who appear in this letter (Colossians 4:9, 17). Philemon was wealthy enough to own at least one slave and to host a congregation in his house, the normal meeting place for churches before there were church buildings.

Slavery in the Roman world was pervasive and was not based on race. People became slaves through capture in war, piracy, debt, being born to an enslaved mother, or being abandoned as infants. Estimates of how much of the population was enslaved vary widely. Slaves worked as field hands and miners but also as household servants, teachers, doctors, and business managers, and freeing slaves (manumission) was common, especially in cities. None of this made the institution gentle. A slave was legally property, could be beaten, sold, or separated from family, and had no right to marry in law. A runaway could be hunted, branded, or worse. Roman legal writers, whose opinions were later gathered in Justinian's Digest, distinguished a fugitive from a slave who left to seek out a friend of the master to plead on his behalf, and some scholars think that distinction may describe Onesimus.
purpose: Paul writes to secure a welcome for Onesimus and a reconciliation between him and Philemon on a new footing. What exactly Paul hoped for is debated. At the least he asks that Philemon receive Onesimus as a brother and not punish him. Verse 13 and the remark that Philemon will do "even more than I ask" (verse 21) suggest to many readers that Paul hoped Onesimus would be freed or sent back to assist him in his work. How Onesimus came to be with Paul is also debated. The traditional view, found in early interpreters such as John Chrysostom, is that he ran away, perhaps after stealing (verse 18). Others think he sought Paul out as a friend of his master to intercede in a dispute, or that Philemon had sent him to Paul. John Knox (1935) argued that the owner was actually Archippus. Allen Dwight Callahan has argued that Onesimus was not a slave at all but Philemon's estranged brother, a reading most scholars have not followed.
story: Philemon comes after the Pastoral Letters in the order of the English Bible, which arranges Paul's letters to churches first and then his letters to individuals, roughly by length. In the story of the early church it belongs with Colossians: the same messengers, Tychicus and Onesimus, probably carried both letters to the Lycus valley. It shows in miniature what Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11 state in principle, that in Christ the categories of slave and free no longer define who a person is before God or in the church. Its questions about how the gospel works on social institutions carry forward through the whole history of the church.
christ: The letter never explains the gospel in the abstract; it acts it out. Paul places himself between the offended master and the guilty or vulnerable slave and says, "charge it to my account" (verse 18). Readers from Martin Luther onward have seen in that sentence a picture of what Christ does for sinners, taking their debt on himself and presenting them to the Father as he would present himself. That is an analogy, not an allegory Paul intended, but it rests on the pattern of his theology. More directly, the phrase "in Christ" and "in the Lord" runs through the letter: it is union with Christ that makes Onesimus Paul's child, Philemon's brother, and a partner in the church.
reading: Read Philemon aloud in one sitting and listen to its tact. It is a real letter to real people, and its persuasion works through courtesy, wordplay, friendship, and public accountability rather than direct command. Watch for the wordplay. Onesimus means ‘useful’ or ‘beneficial’, and verse 11 says he was once achrēstos, ‘useless’, but is now euchrēstos, ‘useful’, words that may also have sounded like Christos, since chrēstos and Christos were pronounced alike in the Greek of the day. In verse 20 Paul asks for ‘benefit’ with onaimēn, a verb from the same root as the name. Watch too for the language of debt, partnership, and refreshed hearts. The standard ancient parallel is a letter of Pliny the Younger to his friend Sabinianus (Letters 9.21), pleading for a freedman who had offended him; set side by side, Pliny appeals to the master's mercy and the man's remorse, while Paul appeals to a new relationship in Christ. Some later history may also be in view. Ignatius of Antioch, writing to the Ephesians in the early second century, names their bishop Onesimus, and John Knox argued that he was the former slave of this letter and that he helped gather Paul's letters, which would explain why so short a note survived; the identification is possible but unproven. Two misreadings should be avoided. One treats the letter as an endorsement of slavery because Paul sends Onesimus back and does not denounce the institution. The other reads it as a direct command to emancipate, which Paul never quite states. The letter is better read as the gospel planting within a household a relationship that the institution of slavery could not contain.

structure.summary: Paul the prisoner and Timothy greet Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church in Philemon's house.

structure.title: Thanksgiving for Philemon's love
structure.summary: Paul thanks God for Philemon's faith and for the love that has refreshed the hearts of the saints, preparing the ground for his request.

structure.title: The appeal for Onesimus
structure.summary: Paul appeals rather than commands, sends Onesimus back as his own heart, asks Philemon to receive him as a beloved brother, and offers to pay whatever he owes.

themes.title: A new relationship in Christ
themes.body: The heart of the letter is verse 16: Onesimus returns "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother." The social arrangement has not yet changed, but the relationship inside it has been redefined. Philemon and Onesimus now share one Lord, one table, and one family, and Paul asks Philemon to let that new reality govern how he treats the man who belongs to him in law.

themes.title: Persuasion through love
themes.body: Paul says he could order Philemon to do the right thing but prefers to appeal "on the basis of love" (verse 9). He wants Philemon's goodness to be freely given, not forced (verse 14). The letter models a kind of authority that refuses to coerce and instead calls on a friend's own faith, while still being frank about what is expected.

themes.title: Substitution and debt
themes.body: Paul steps in to cover whatever Onesimus owes and writes the pledge in his own hand. The language of accounts, debts, and repayment turns a legal matter into an act of costly friendship. Christians have long heard in it an echo of the substitution at the heart of the gospel.

themes.title: The gospel and social institutions
themes.body: Philemon raises a question the church has argued about ever since: does the gospel only change hearts within existing structures, or does it undermine unjust structures themselves? The letter was quoted on both sides of the American debate over slavery. Most readers today see in it a seed whose logic, a slave who is a brother "in the Lord" and "in person", could not in the end coexist with ownership of one person by another.

keyChapters.why: The whole letter is one chapter: Paul's appeal for Onesimus, a slave who has become a brother, and his offer to take on Onesimus's debt himself.

parts.body:
Philemon is Paul's shortest letter, a single page, and it can be read aloud in about three minutes. It has only one chapter.

Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a believer who has a church meeting in his house. He writes about one man: Onesimus, a slave who belonged to Philemon. Onesimus has come to faith in Christ through Paul while Paul was in chains, and Paul is now sending him back to Philemon.

The whole letter is a request for how Philemon should receive him. Paul could give an order, and says so, but he chooses to appeal ‘on the basis of love’ (verse 9). He asks Philemon to take Onesimus back “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (verse 16), and even to “receive him as you would receive me” (verse 17). If Onesimus owes anything, “charge it to my account” (verse 18).

The letter is small, but it reaches into the most unequal relationship in a Roman house, between an owner and a person he owned, and refuses to leave it as it was. It also has a long and painful history. For centuries people used it to send enslaved people back to their masters. These notes name that misuse plainly, and they set out fairly what the letter says, what it does not say, and how readers have understood what Paul hoped for.

Paul names himself, with Timothy, at the start (verse 1), and he writes part of the letter with his own hand (verse 19). Few letters in the New Testament are as secure. Even scholars who doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, Ephesians or the Pastoral Letters count Philemon among the seven letters nearly everyone accepts as his.

It was in Marcion's list of Paul's letters in the second century, and in the Muratorian list, usually dated to the late second century. Because it is so short and so personal, a few in the 300s asked whether it belonged in Scripture at all. Writers such as Jerome and John Chrysostom defended it, arguing that small letters can carry large truths.

Paul says four times that he is a prisoner (verses 1, 9, 10, 13), but he does not say where.

The traditional view is that he wrote from Rome, where he was under guard for two years at the end of Acts, around AD 60 to 62. That would make Philemon a companion of Colossians, which was carried on the same trip, and perhaps of Ephesians and Philippians.

Many scholars prefer Ephesus, in the mid-50s. Ephesus is only about 120 miles (190 km) from Colossae, which makes it easier to picture Onesimus reaching Paul, and Paul hoping to visit soon (verse 22). Acts does not tell of Paul being imprisoned in Ephesus, but Paul speaks of ‘more imprisonments’ than others had known (2 Corinthians 11:23). A smaller number suggest Caesarea, around AD 57 to 59.

The meaning of the letter does not depend on settling this. These notes do not choose.

parts.h: Philemon, Onesimus, and the church in his house: what is known, and what readers infer
parts.body:
Here it helps to keep apart what the letter says and what readers have worked out.

What the letter says. Philemon is a ‘beloved fellow worker’ (verse 1), and a church meets in his house (verse 2). His love has ‘refreshed the hearts of the saints’ (verse 7). Paul says Philemon owes him ‘your very self’ (verse 19), which many take to mean that Philemon came to faith through Paul. Apphia, ‘our sister’, and Archippus, ‘our fellow soldier’, are greeted too (verse 2). Onesimus belonged to Philemon as a slave (verse 16). He was ‘separated from you for a while’ (verse 15). He came to faith through Paul while Paul was in chains: ‘my child Onesimus, whose father I became’ (verse 10). Paul is sending him back (verse 12). And Paul says, ‘if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account’ (verse 18).

What readers infer. That Philemon lived at Colossae comes from Colossians, which calls Onesimus ‘one of you’ and sends a message to Archippus (Colossians 4:9, 17). How Onesimus came to be with Paul is not stated. Many read the letter, as early interpreters such as John Chrysostom did, to mean that he ran away, perhaps after stealing something, and verse 18 is the reason. Others note that Roman legal writers, whose opinions were later gathered in Justinian's Digest, distinguished a runaway from a slave who went to a friend of his master to ask him to plead his case, and some read Onesimus that way: he went to Paul for help in a quarrel with Philemon. Others again think Philemon had sent Onesimus to help Paul. Each view explains some details and strains at others. The letter does not say that Onesimus ran away, and it does not say that he stole.

What a slave's life was. Roman slavery was not based on race, and freeing slaves was common in the cities. But a slave was property in law. He could be beaten, sold, or separated from his family, and a runaway could be hunted, branded or worse. If he had run away, he was going back into real danger, and Paul would have known it.

Greeting (verses 1-3). Paul ‘a prisoner of Christ Jesus’ and Timothy write to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church in Philemon's house. The whole church will hear the letter.

Thanks (verses 4-7). Paul thanks God for Philemon's faith and love, and for how he has ‘refreshed the hearts of the saints’.

The appeal (verses 8-22). Paul could order but prefers to appeal. He names Onesimus, plays on his name, sends him back as ‘my very heart’, asks that he be received as a brother and as Paul himself, offers to pay what he owes, and is sure Philemon will do ‘even more than I ask’. Prepare a guest room: Paul hopes to come.

Greetings and blessing (verses 23-25). Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke send greetings. Grace be with your spirit.

Notice how Paul waits. He does not name Onesimus until verse 10, after he has praised Philemon's love and described himself as old and in chains. And the letter ends where it began: Philemon has refreshed the hearts of the saints (verse 7); now ‘refresh my heart in Christ’ (verse 20).

parts.h: What Paul asks, and what he does not say
parts.body:
Paul's request is plain. Receive Onesimus. Receive him “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (verse 16). Receive him ‘as you would receive me’ (verse 17). Do not hold any debt against him; put it on Paul's account (verse 18). And do it freely: “so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will” (verse 14).

Notice ‘both in person and in the Lord’ (verse 16). Paul does not say Onesimus is a brother only at church, on Sunday, while he stays property the rest of the week. He is a brother in everyday life too. That is the sentence that put a crack in the whole arrangement.

What Paul does not say is just as important. He does not say in so many words, ‘Set him free’. He does not say slavery is wrong. Readers should not pretend he does.

So what was he hoping Philemon would do? Readers have answered in three main ways. Many read the letter as asking at least that Philemon welcome Onesimus back without punishment, as a brother in Christ, and treat him from now on as one. Many read verse 16 and ‘you will do even more than I ask’ (verse 21) as Paul's tactful way of asking Philemon to free him. And many read verse 13, ‘I would have liked to keep him with me’, as a hint that Paul hoped Philemon would send Onesimus back to help him in his work. These readings can overlap, and these notes do not choose.

We do not know what Philemon did. Some readers take the fact that the letter was kept, copied and read in the churches as a sign that he did what Paul asked. Some think the Onesimus whom Ignatius of Antioch, early in the second century, names as bishop of Ephesus was the same man. That is possible, but it cannot be proved.

parts.h: The letter and slavery: a misuse named
parts.body:
This letter's history is painful, and it has to be faced.

In the years before the American Civil War, defenders of slavery cited Philemon as proof that the apostle sent a runaway back to his master. They used it to support the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, a law requiring that people who had escaped slavery be returned, and to defend slavery itself as biblical. That was a misuse of this letter, and it was wrong. Paul sent Onesimus back ‘no longer as a slave’ and ‘as a beloved brother’, with his own name and money put on the line for him. And the law of Moses itself had said, “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you” (Deuteronomy 23:15). And Atlantic slavery, built on race and kidnapping, was very different from the Roman kind; the law of Moses punished kidnapping with death (Exodus 21:16).

Abolitionists answered from the same letter: a master who took verse 16 seriously could not keep treating his brother as property. Enslaved Christians themselves often heard the Bible very differently from the way it was preached to them.

Why did Paul not say more? He was a prisoner with no power over Roman law, writing to a tiny community, and an open call for slaves to be freed could have brought violent suspicion on the church. But the letter plants something that slavery could not hold for ever: a slave who is a brother ‘in person and in the Lord’, a master who owes his slave a welcome, and both standing equal in one church. Later Christians drew that out. Gregory of Nyssa, in the 300s, preached against owning human beings at all, and the evangelical abolitionists of the 1700s and 1800s drew out the same rejection of the institution. The church was slow, and its slowness is part of its history to be confessed, not defended.

Nor is this letter a lesson about any party or any modern policy. It is a letter about how two believers, one with power and one without, are to treat each other because both belong to Christ.

In verse 18 Paul steps between the two men. Whatever Onesimus owes, Paul will pay. And to make it binding, he takes the pen himself: “I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it” (verse 19). It was like signing an IOU.

Readers from Martin Luther onward have seen in this a picture of what Christ does. Luther, in his preface to the letter, said in effect that we are all Christ's Onesimus: Christ takes our debt on himself and asks the Father to receive us as he would receive him. That is a comparison drawn from Paul's teaching, not a hidden meaning Paul put in the letter. But it fits. Paul is acting out, on a small scale, the gospel he preached.

Notice too how Paul uses his power. He could command (verse 8). He chooses to ask, to pay, and to trust. Power held this way does not crush the weak. It spends itself for them.

A new family in Christ. Onesimus is Paul's ‘child’ (verse 10), Philemon's ‘brother’ (verse 16), and Paul's ‘very heart’ (verse 12). Faith in Christ makes people family across every line the world draws. In another letter Paul writes, “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

Love that persuades. Paul appeals rather than commands, so that Philemon's goodness will be free. Love does not force, but it does not stay vague either. Paul says plainly what he wants.

Partnership. The Greek word koinōnia, ‘partnership’ or ‘fellowship’, appears in verse 6, and its partner word in verse 17: ‘if you consider me a partner’. Sharing faith means sharing life, and even sharing debts.

Refreshed hearts. The word for ‘heart’ in verses 7, 12 and 20 means the deepest feelings. Philemon has refreshed others; now Paul asks him to refresh Paul's heart by welcoming Onesimus.

The gospel and the structures of the world. Does the gospel only change hearts inside unjust arrangements, or does it work against the arrangements themselves? This letter has been argued over on that question for centuries. Most readers today see in it a seed whose growth could not, in the end, live alongside one person owning another.

The letter quotes no Old Testament verse, but it stands on Israel's law and wisdom.

The law protected a slave who escaped: “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you. Let him live among you wherever he chooses, in the town of his pleasing. Do not oppress him” (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). It made kidnapping a person a capital crime (Exodus 21:16). And it reminded Israel why: “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (Deuteronomy 15:15).

It told Israelites not to treat a fellow Israelite who sold himself into service as a slave: “Let him stay with you as a hired worker” (Leviticus 25:40).

And Job said why he could not treat his servants as less than himself: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” (Job 31:15).

It is not a defence of slavery, and it was never a warrant for sending anyone back into slavery. People who used it that way misused it.

It is not a report that Onesimus was a thief or a runaway. The letter does not say either. Those are readings, some old and widely held, and they may be right, but the text leaves the question open.

It is not a direct command to set Onesimus free, and it should not be made to say more than it says. Its force is in what it asks and what it hints.

It is not a rule about work today. An employee is not property, and no one should use this letter to tell anyone to stay in a place where they are mistreated.

And it is not a lesson for any party. It is a letter about two believers learning to be brothers.

Read it aloud, in one sitting, and listen to its tact. Picture it being read in Philemon's house, in front of the whole church, perhaps with Onesimus standing there.

Listen for the wordplay. The name Onesimus means ‘useful’. Paul says he was once ‘useless’ but is now ‘useful’ (verse 11), and in verse 20 asks Philemon for ‘benefit’ with a word from the same root as the name. In the Greek of the day, the word for ‘useful’ also sounded much like ‘Christ’.

Watch for the words of family (child, brother, sister), of heart, of partnership, and of accounts and debts.

Where readers differ, about what Onesimus had done and what Paul hoped for, read the case for each before you settle.

And let the letter ask you its questions. Who is the person you find hardest to receive as a brother or sister? Where do you hold power over someone, and how are you using it? Whose debt could you put on your own account? And is there anyone you are keeping at a distance whom Christ calls family?

The note on the chapter goes through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: Onesimus. What the letter says about him, and what readers have inferred about how he came to Paul.
‘No longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother.’ Why Paul did not command freedom, and the misuse of this letter.
‘Charge it to my account.’ Paul's pledge, and a picture of the gospel.
‘Even more than I ask.’ The main readings of what Paul hoped Philemon would do.

words.line: A common slave name meaning ‘useful’ or ‘beneficial’, the kind of name an owner gave (verse 10).
Greek achrēstos and euchrēstos. Paul's play on the name, which may also have sounded like Christos (verse 11).
Greek doulos, a person owned by another. Onesimus returns ‘no longer as a slave’ (verse 16).
Greek koinōnia, shared life, shared faith, even shared debt (verses 6, 17).
Greek splanchna, the inner parts, the seat of the deepest feelings (verses 7, 12, 20).
Paul could order but chooses to ask, ‘on the basis of love’ (verses 8-10).

places.name: Rome
places.line: Where Paul lived under guard two years (Acts 28:30). The traditional view is that he wrote from here, ‘a prisoner of Christ Jesus’ (verse 1).
